topic: Pediatrics: AOM amoxicillin high-dose, fever dosing APAP/ibuprofen
front: 2-year-old, 12 kg, acute otitis media, no recent antibiotics. Dose? Fever options?
bottom: High-dose amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day divided BID.

bullets.clue: 12 kg × 90 = 1080 mg/day → 540 mg BID. Amox/clav if amoxicillin in past 30 days.
bullets.treat: Fever: acetaminophen 15 mg/kg q4–6h; ibuprofen 10 mg/kg q6–8h.
bullets.trap: No ibuprofen under 6 months.

back: High-dose amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day divided BID. Key clue: 12 kg × 90 = 1080 mg/day → 540 mg BID. Amox/clav if amoxicillin in past 30 days. Pharmacist move: Fever: acetaminophen 15 mg/kg q4–6h; ibuprofen 10 mg/kg q6–8h. Exam trap: No ibuprofen under 6 months.

source.guideline: AAP 2013 AOM (latest AAP AOM guideline; due for AAP review)
source.recommendation: AAP 2013 AOM guideline: amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses first-line; amoxicillin-clavulanate if amoxicillin within 30 days, concurrent purulent conjunctivitis, or recurrent AOM unresponsive to amoxicillin; observation option for selected children. Labeling: acetaminophen 15 mg/kg q4–6h; ibuprofen 10 mg/kg q6–8h, not under 6 months without prescriber.

topic: Pregnancy: GDM insulin/metformin, HTN in pregnancy (labetalol, nifedipine), low-dose aspirin
front: Pregnant with chronic HTN (BP 145/92) and high preeclampsia risk. Drugs?
bottom: Labetalol or nifedipine ER, plus aspirin 81 mg.

bullets.clue: Treat BP ≥140/90 in pregnancy (CHAP).
bullets.treat: Aspirin 81 mg daily from 12 weeks until delivery; GDM: insulin preferred.
bullets.trap: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy.

back: Labetalol or nifedipine ER, plus aspirin 81 mg. Key clue: Treat BP ≥140/90 in pregnancy (CHAP). Pharmacist move: Aspirin 81 mg daily from 12 weeks until delivery; GDM: insulin preferred. Exam trap: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy.

source.guideline: ACOG CPU 2024 GDM screening + PB 190 (reaffirmed); ACOG PB 222 2020 + 2022 CHAP advisory; USPSTF 2021 aspirin
source.recommendation: ACOG 2022 CHAP practice advisory: treat chronic hypertension in pregnancy at ≥140/90; labetalol and nifedipine preferred; ACOG PB 222. USPSTF 2021: low-dose aspirin 81 mg/day after 12 weeks for high preeclampsia risk. ACOG PB 190: insulin preferred for GDM pharmacotherapy. ACEi/ARBs contraindicated (fetotoxicity).

topic: Pain: acetaminophen max dose, NSAID selection by GI/CV risk
front: Arthritis patient with prior GI bleed and high CV risk asks about NSAIDs. Advice?
bottom: Avoid NSAIDs: high GI and high CV risk.

bullets.clue: High GI risk alone: celecoxib plus a PPI. High CV risk alone: naproxen plus PPI if GI risk.
bullets.treat: Acetaminophen max 4 g/day; lower (e.g., 3 g) with liver disease or heavy alcohol use.
bullets.trap: Check OTC combination products for hidden acetaminophen.

back: Avoid NSAIDs: high GI and high CV risk. Key clue: High GI risk alone: celecoxib plus a PPI. High CV risk alone: naproxen plus PPI if GI risk. Pharmacist move: Acetaminophen max 4 g/day; lower (e.g., 3 g) with liver disease or heavy alcohol use. Exam trap: Check OTC combination products for hidden acetaminophen.

source.recommendation: ACG 2009 NSAID-related ulcer prevention: high GI risk—avoid NSAIDs or use COX-2 inhibitor plus PPI; CV risk requiring aspirin—naproxen plus PPI; high GI and CV risk—avoid NSAIDs. Acetaminophen labeling: max 4 g/day; liver warning with ≥3 alcoholic drinks/day; avoid duplicate acetaminophen products. CDC 2022: nonopioid therapies preferred.

topic: OTC self-care exclusions: cough/cold in <4 y, pseudoephedrine limits
front: Parent wants OTC cough syrup for a 3-year-old and pseudoephedrine for themself. Rules?
bottom: No OTC cough/cold under 4 (label); pseudoephedrine behind the counter.

bullets.clue: FDA: don't use under 2; labels say don't use under 4.
bullets.treat: Pseudoephedrine: max 3.6 g/day and 9 g/30 days; photo ID and logbook.
bullets.trap: Honey (age ≥1) is a non-drug option for cough.

back: No OTC cough/cold under 4 (label); pseudoephedrine behind the counter. Key clue: FDA: don't use under 2; labels say don't use under 4. Pharmacist move: Pseudoephedrine: max 3.6 g/day and 9 g/30 days; photo ID and logbook. Exam trap: Honey (age ≥1) is a non-drug option for cough.

source.recommendation: FDA 2008 public health advisory: OTC cough and cold products should not be used in children under 2; manufacturers voluntarily relabeled 'do not use in children under 4'. Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act 2005: pseudoephedrine behind counter, 3.6 g/day and 9 g/30-day purchase limits, ID and logbook.

topic: Dermatology: acne topical retinoid/BPO; isotretinoin
front: Moderate acne on topical clindamycin alone. What's wrong, and isotretinoin rules?
bottom: Never use a topical antibiotic alone: add benzoyl peroxide.

bullets.clue: First-line: topical retinoid plus BPO, with or without topical antibiotic.
bullets.treat: Isotretinoin: iPLEDGE REMS, pregnancy tests and two forms of contraception.
bullets.trap: Limit oral doxycycline courses; always pair with topicals.

back: Never use a topical antibiotic alone: add benzoyl peroxide. Key clue: First-line: topical retinoid plus BPO, with or without topical antibiotic. Pharmacist move: Isotretinoin: iPLEDGE REMS, pregnancy tests and two forms of contraception. Exam trap: Limit oral doxycycline courses; always pair with topicals.

source.recommendation: AAD 2024 acne guideline: benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics (combined with BPO, not monotherapy), oral doxycycline with limited duration; isotretinoin for severe/refractory acne. Isotretinoin labeling: iPLEDGE REMS, two forms of contraception and pregnancy testing.

topic: Public health screening & pharmacist-prescribed naloxone/contraception
front: Caregiver asks for naloxone without a patient-specific prescription. Can you provide it?
bottom: Yes: via standing order/protocol, or OTC.

bullets.clue: Every state allows pharmacist naloxone access by standing order or protocol.
bullets.treat: Hormonal contraception and other prescribing depend on state law.
bullets.trap: Scope varies by state: check your board's protocol.

back: Yes: via standing order/protocol, or OTC. Key clue: Every state allows pharmacist naloxone access by standing order or protocol. Pharmacist move: Hormonal contraception and other prescribing depend on state law. Exam trap: Scope varies by state: check your board's protocol.

source.guideline: CDC 2022; USPSTF current recommendations; state protocols
source.recommendation: CDC 2022: offer naloxone to patients at increased overdose risk; all states permit pharmacist naloxone dispensing via standing orders, protocols or prescriptive authority; 4 mg nasal naloxone OTC since 2023. Pharmacist prescribing of hormonal contraception per state law. USPSTF current recommendations for screening.

topic: Medication take-back & safe disposal of opioids
front: Patient brings leftover oxycodone to the counter. Can you take it?
bottom: Only into an authorized collection receptacle.

bullets.clue: Pharmacies may register with DEA as collectors; it's voluntary.
bullets.treat: No take-back nearby: FDA flush list drugs (e.g., fentanyl patches) can be flushed; otherwise mix with coffee grounds and seal.
bullets.trap: Staff can't count, sort or handle receptacle contents.

back: Only into an authorized collection receptacle. Key clue: Pharmacies may register with DEA as collectors; it's voluntary. Pharmacist move: No take-back nearby: FDA flush list drugs (e.g., fentanyl patches) can be flushed; otherwise mix with coffee grounds and seal. Exam trap: Staff can't count, sort or handle receptacle contents.

source.guideline: DEA Disposal Rule 21 CFR 1317; FDA flush list
source.recommendation: DEA Disposal Rule (21 CFR 1317): retail pharmacies may register as collectors and maintain collection receptacles; patients deposit controlled substances directly; staff may not count, sort or inventory contents. FDA: flush list for select high-risk medicines when take-back unavailable; otherwise mix with unappealing substance and seal in trash.

topic: Patient privacy: HIPAA permitted disclosures
front: Patient's daughter picks up the Rx and asks what it's for. Can you share?
bottom: Yes, if she's involved in care and the patient doesn't object.

bullets.clue: Treatment, payment and operations need no written authorization.
bullets.treat: Minimum necessary applies, except for treatment disclosures.
bullets.trap: The 2024 reproductive-health privacy rule was vacated in 2025.

back: Yes, if she's involved in care and the patient doesn't object. Key clue: Treatment, payment and operations need no written authorization. Pharmacist move: Minimum necessary applies, except for treatment disclosures. Exam trap: The 2024 reproductive-health privacy rule was vacated in 2025.

source.guideline: HIPAA Privacy Rule 45 CFR 164 (2024 reproductive-health rule vacated Jun 2025)
source.recommendation: HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 CFR 164.506, 164.510, 164.502(b)): disclosures for treatment, payment, health care operations without authorization; disclosures to family involved in care if patient does not object or professional judgment; minimum necessary standard (not applicable to treatment). 2024 reproductive health care privacy amendments vacated by federal court June 2025.

topic: Informed consent, autonomy & refusal of therapy
front: Competent patient refuses the statin you recommended. What do you do?
bottom: Respect the refusal: autonomy.

bullets.clue: Explain benefits, risks and alternatives in plain language.
bullets.treat: Document the discussion and inform the prescriber.
bullets.trap: Pressure or deception violates the Code of Ethics.

back: Respect the refusal: autonomy. Key clue: Explain benefits, risks and alternatives in plain language. Pharmacist move: Document the discussion and inform the prescriber. Exam trap: Pressure or deception violates the Code of Ethics.

source.recommendation: APhA Code of Ethics: pharmacist respects the autonomy and dignity of each patient, promotes the right of self-determination, and encourages patients to participate in decisions about their health; informed decision-making requires disclosure of benefits, risks and alternatives.

topic: Conscientious objection & duty to ensure access
front: You object to dispensing a medication on moral grounds. What's required?
bottom: Step away, but ensure the patient still gets it.

bullets.clue: APhA policy: pharmacist may decline if a system ensures patient access.
bullets.treat: Arrange transfer to a colleague or another pharmacy without delay.
bullets.trap: State laws vary; never obstruct, lecture or withhold the prescription.

back: Step away, but ensure the patient still gets it. Key clue: APhA policy: pharmacist may decline if a system ensures patient access. Pharmacist move: Arrange transfer to a colleague or another pharmacy without delay. Exam trap: State laws vary; never obstruct, lecture or withhold the prescription.

source.guideline: APhA Code of Ethics; APhA conscience policy (1998)
source.recommendation: APhA 1998 policy: recognizes the individual pharmacist's right to exercise conscientious refusal and supports systems to ensure the patient's access to legally prescribed therapy without compromising the pharmacist's right. State laws vary.

topic: Medication error disclosure & reporting (MedWatch, ISMP MERP, VAERS)
front: Wrong drug dispensed; patient had a reaction. And a separate vaccine reaction. Where to report?
bottom: Disclose to patient; MedWatch/ISMP for the error; VAERS for vaccine.

bullets.clue: ISMP MERP: voluntary, confidential error reporting.
bullets.treat: MedWatch: serious adverse events and product problems.
bullets.trap: Vaccine adverse events go to VAERS, not MedWatch.

back: Disclose to patient; MedWatch/ISMP for the error; VAERS for vaccine. Key clue: ISMP MERP: voluntary, confidential error reporting. Pharmacist move: MedWatch: serious adverse events and product problems. Exam trap: Vaccine adverse events go to VAERS, not MedWatch.

source.recommendation: FDA MedWatch for serious adverse events, product quality problems and medication errors; ISMP National Medication Errors Reporting Program (MERP) voluntary reporting; VAERS for adverse events after vaccination (required reporting of certain events by providers). Disclosure of errors to patients is an ethical expectation.

topic: Impaired colleague reporting
front: Coworker smells of alcohol and is checking prescriptions. Your duty?
bottom: Act now: protect patients, then report.

bullets.clue: Remove the colleague from patient care; tell the supervisor or pharmacist-in-charge.
bullets.treat: Refer to the state's pharmacist recovery (PRN) program or board per law.
bullets.trap: Covering for a colleague puts patients at risk.

back: Act now: protect patients, then report. Key clue: Remove the colleague from patient care; tell the supervisor or pharmacist-in-charge. Pharmacist move: Refer to the state's pharmacist recovery (PRN) program or board per law. Exam trap: Covering for a colleague puts patients at risk.

source.guideline: APhA Code of Ethics; state PRN programs
source.recommendation: APhA Code of Ethics: pharmacist acts with honesty and integrity and exposes, when necessary, incompetent or unethical conduct; state boards and pharmacist recovery network (PRN) programs provide pathways for impaired practitioners.

topic: Health literacy, teach-back & limited English proficiency interpreters
front: Patient with limited English nods along. Best counseling approach?
bottom: Qualified interpreter plus teach-back.

bullets.clue: Teach-back: patient explains in their own words how to take it.
bullets.treat: Use plain language and focus on 2–3 key points.
bullets.trap: Don't use family members or children as interpreters.

back: Qualified interpreter plus teach-back. Key clue: Teach-back: patient explains in their own words how to take it. Pharmacist move: Use plain language and focus on 2–3 key points. Exam trap: Don't use family members or children as interpreters.

source.guideline: AHRQ Health Literacy Toolkit 2024; Title VI
source.recommendation: AHRQ Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit (3rd ed., 2024): teach-back, plain language, limit key messages; Title VI of the Civil Rights Act: language assistance for LEP individuals using qualified interpreters; avoid relying on family/minors.

topic: Cultural/social determinants and adherence barriers
front: Patient skips insulin doses because of cost. Which PPCP step finds this, and what next?
bottom: Collect/Assess: ask about barriers, then plan.

bullets.clue: PPCP: Collect, Assess, Plan, Implement, Follow-up.
bullets.treat: Address cost: lower-cost insulin, $35 Medicare cap, assistance programs.
bullets.trap: Ask open-ended, nonjudgmental questions.

back: Collect/Assess: ask about barriers, then plan. Key clue: PPCP: Collect, Assess, Plan, Implement, Follow-up. Pharmacist move: Address cost: lower-cost insulin, $35 Medicare cap, assistance programs. Exam trap: Ask open-ended, nonjudgmental questions.

source.recommendation: JCPP Pharmacists' Patient Care Process: Collect, Assess, Plan, Implement, Follow-up (monitor and evaluate), patient-centered and addressing social determinants and adherence barriers. Inflation Reduction Act: Medicare insulin cost-sharing capped at $35/month.

topic: Collaborative practice agreements & pharmacist prescribing scope
front: Under a collaborative practice agreement, what can a pharmacist do?
bottom: Functions defined in a written protocol with a prescriber.

bullets.clue: Often: initiate, modify or stop therapy and order labs.
bullets.treat: Scope, patients and drugs depend on state law and the agreement.
bullets.trap: A CPA isn't independent prescriptive authority.

back: Functions defined in a written protocol with a prescriber. Key clue: Often: initiate, modify or stop therapy and order labs. Pharmacist move: Scope, patients and drugs depend on state law and the agreement. Exam trap: A CPA isn't independent prescriptive authority.

source.recommendation: CDC collaborative practice resources; state CPA laws: written agreement between pharmacist and prescriber defining delegated functions (initiating, modifying, discontinuing therapy, ordering tests) under protocol; scope varies by state. JCPP PPCP.

topic: Inventory: turnover rate, par levels, ABC analysis
front: Calc: annual cost of goods sold $1,800,000; inventory $160,000 at start, $140,000 at end. Turnover rate and days on hand?
bottom: 12 turns/year; ~30 days of inventory.

bullets.trap: Use cost of goods sold, not sales revenue.

back: 12 turns/year; ~30 days of inventory. Given: Average inventory = (160,000 + 140,000) ÷ 2 = $150,000. Work: Turnover = 1,800,000 ÷ 150,000 = 12. Days = 365 ÷ 12 ≈ 30.4. Exam trap: Use cost of goods sold, not sales revenue.

source.recommendation: Standard pharmacy management formula: inventory turnover rate = cost of goods sold ÷ average inventory (at cost); average inventory = (beginning + ending) ÷ 2; days' supply on hand = 365 ÷ turnover rate.

topic: Drug shortages management
front: Critical drug goes on shortage. Pharmacy's first steps?
bottom: Assess supply and find alternatives.

bullets.clue: Check on-hand stock, usage rate, and FDA/ASHP shortage lists.
bullets.treat: P&T sets therapeutic alternatives and allocation rules; communicate to prescribers.
bullets.trap: Don't hoard or buy from unverified gray-market sellers.

back: Assess supply and find alternatives. Key clue: Check on-hand stock, usage rate, and FDA/ASHP shortage lists. Pharmacist move: P&T sets therapeutic alternatives and allocation rules; communicate to prescribers. Exam trap: Don't hoard or buy from unverified gray-market sellers.

source.guideline: ASHP Drug Shortages Guidelines 2018 (still current, latest = 2018)
source.recommendation: ASHP Guidelines on Managing Drug Product Shortages (2018): operational and therapeutic assessment, identify alternatives, P&T-approved allocation/conservation strategies, communication, avoid hoarding and purchasing from unauthorized sources.

topic: DSCSA traceability (enhanced security Nov 2024)
front: Suspect counterfeit product arrives. What does DSCSA require?
bottom: Quarantine and investigate.

bullets.clue: Buy only from authorized trading partners; keep transaction data.
bullets.treat: If illegitimate, notify FDA (Form 3911) and partners within 24 hours.
bullets.trap: Small dispensers (≤25 FTE) are exempt from electronic interoperability until Nov 27, 2027.

back: Quarantine and investigate. Key clue: Buy only from authorized trading partners; keep transaction data. Pharmacist move: If illegitimate, notify FDA (Form 3911) and partners within 24 hours. Exam trap: Small dispensers (≤25 FTE) are exempt from electronic interoperability until Nov 27, 2027.

source.guideline: FDA DSCSA; small-dispenser exemption to Nov 27, 2027
source.recommendation: DSCSA: dispensers must transact with authorized trading partners, maintain transaction information, quarantine and investigate suspect product, notify FDA (Form 3911) and trading partners within 24 hours of determining illegitimate product; enhanced drug distribution security requirements from Nov 27, 2024 with FDA exemptions; small dispensers (≤25 full-time pharmacists/technicians) exempt until Nov 27, 2027.

topic: Recalls: Class I/II/III and pharmacy response
front: FDA recall: 'reasonable probability of serious harm or death.' Which class?
bottom: Class I.

bullets.clue: Class II: temporary or reversible harm. Class III: unlikely to cause harm.
bullets.treat: Pull affected lots; contact patients when the recall reaches consumer level.
bullets.trap: Market withdrawal isn't a recall: no FDA violation.

back: Class I. Key clue: Class II: temporary or reversible harm. Class III: unlikely to cause harm. Pharmacist move: Pull affected lots; contact patients when the recall reaches consumer level. Exam trap: Market withdrawal isn't a recall: no FDA violation.

source.recommendation: 21 CFR 7.3: Class I—reasonable probability of serious adverse health consequences or death; Class II—temporary or medically reversible consequences, remote probability of serious harm; Class III—not likely to cause adverse health consequences; market withdrawal involves minor or no violation.

topic: Controlled substance ordering, DEA 222/CSOS, inventory, theft (Form 106)
front: Ordering oxycodone, taking inventory, and finding a theft. Which forms and rules?
bottom: DEA Form 222 or CSOS; theft: Form 106.

bullets.clue: Biennial inventory: exact count for CII; estimate CIII–V unless container >1,000 units.
bullets.treat: Report theft to the DEA field office within 1 business day, then file Form 106.
bullets.trap: Keep controlled substance records at least 2 years.

back: DEA Form 222 or CSOS; theft: Form 106. Key clue: Biennial inventory: exact count for CII; estimate CIII–V unless container >1,000 units. Pharmacist move: Report theft to the DEA field office within 1 business day, then file Form 106. Exam trap: Keep controlled substance records at least 2 years.

source.recommendation: 21 CFR 1305: Schedule I–II orders via DEA Form 222 or CSOS. 21 CFR 1304.11: biennial inventory—exact count for Schedule I–II, estimated count for III–V unless container holds >1,000 units; 1304.04: records kept 2 years. 21 CFR 1301.76(b): notify DEA in writing within one business day of discovering theft or significant loss and complete DEA Form 106.

topic: Pharmacoeconomics: CMA, CEA, CUA (QALY), CBA
front: Calc: Drug A costs $50,000 for 3.0 QALYs; Drug B $20,000 for 2.5 QALYs. ICER?
bottom: $60,000 per QALY gained.

bullets.clue: ICER = ΔCost ÷ ΔQALY.
bullets.trap: QALYs = cost-utility; outcomes in dollars = cost-benefit.

back: $60,000 per QALY gained. Given: ICER = ΔCost ÷ ΔQALY. Work: (50,000 − 20,000) ÷ (3.0 − 2.5) = 30,000 ÷ 0.5 = $60,000/QALY. Exam trap: QALYs = cost-utility; outcomes in dollars = cost-benefit.

source.recommendation: ISPOR good practices: incremental cost-effectiveness ratio = (Cost A − Cost B) ÷ (Effect A − Effect B); cost-utility analysis measures outcomes in QALYs; cost-benefit analysis values outcomes in monetary units; cost-minimization assumes equal outcomes.

topic: Quality improvement: PDSA, RCA, FMEA
front: Sentinel event vs a new process: which QI tool for each?
bottom: RCA after the event; FMEA before the process.

bullets.clue: RCA is reactive; FMEA proactively ranks failure modes.
bullets.treat: Test changes with small PDSA cycles.
bullets.trap: RCA targets systems, not individual blame.

back: RCA after the event; FMEA before the process. Key clue: RCA is reactive; FMEA proactively ranks failure modes. Pharmacist move: Test changes with small PDSA cycles. Exam trap: RCA targets systems, not individual blame.

source.guideline: IHI Model for Improvement; TJC Sentinel Event Policy 2025
source.recommendation: IHI Model for Improvement: Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles. Joint Commission Sentinel Event Policy (2025): comprehensive systematic analysis (e.g., root cause analysis) and action plan after sentinel events, focused on systems. FMEA is a proactive risk assessment tool.

topic: Medication reconciliation at transitions of care
front: Patient admitted from home. Steps of medication reconciliation?
bottom: Get the best possible list, compare, resolve discrepancies.

bullets.clue: Include OTCs, supplements and doses at every transition.
bullets.treat: At discharge, give the patient an updated list and explain changes.
bullets.trap: Reconcile at admission, transfer and discharge, not only once.

back: Get the best possible list, compare, resolve discrepancies. Key clue: Include OTCs, supplements and doses at every transition. Pharmacist move: At discharge, give the patient an updated list and explain changes. Exam trap: Reconcile at admission, transfer and discharge, not only once.

source.guideline: Joint Commission National Performance Goals 2026 (NPG 14, replaces NPSG.03.06.01)
source.recommendation: Joint Commission National Performance Goals (effective Jan 1, 2026; NPG 14 Effectively Managing Medications, which carries over former NPSG.03.06.01): obtain and document current medications on admission, compare with ordered medications and resolve discrepancies, provide written updated medication information at discharge and educate the patient.

topic: Pharmacy quality measures (PDC ≥80%, star ratings)
front: Plan says a patient's statin adherence is PDC 75%. What's the threshold and formula?
bottom: Adherent = PDC ≥80%.

bullets.clue: PDC = days covered ÷ days in the measurement period.
bullets.treat: Diabetes, RAS antagonist and statin adherence drive Part D Star Ratings.
bullets.trap: PDC doesn't double-count overlapping fills like MPR can.

back: Adherent = PDC ≥80%. Key clue: PDC = days covered ÷ days in the measurement period. Pharmacist move: Diabetes, RAS antagonist and statin adherence drive Part D Star Ratings. Exam trap: PDC doesn't double-count overlapping fills like MPR can.

source.recommendation: PQA measures 2026: proportion of days covered (PDC) ≥80% defines adherence for diabetes medications, RAS antagonists and statins; PDC caps overlapping supply. CMS 2026 Star Ratings include these Part D adherence measures.

topic: Billing: Medicare Part B vs D, 340B basics
front: Medicare patient: flu shot, Shingrix, and oral transplant immunosuppressant. Part B or D?
bottom: Flu: Part B. Shingrix: Part D. Transplant drugs: Part B if Medicare paid for the transplant.

bullets.clue: Part B: flu, pneumococcal, hep B, COVID vaccines; drugs given incident to a physician service.
bullets.treat: Part D covers ACIP vaccines at $0 cost-sharing; out-of-pocket cap $2,100 in 2026.
bullets.trap: 340B: no duplicate Medicaid discounts, no diversion to non-patients.

back: Flu: Part B. Shingrix: Part D. Transplant drugs: Part B if Medicare paid for the transplant. Key clue: Part B: flu, pneumococcal, hep B, COVID vaccines; drugs given incident to a physician service. Pharmacist move: Part D covers ACIP vaccines at $0 cost-sharing; out-of-pocket cap $2,100 in 2026. Exam trap: 340B: no duplicate Medicaid discounts, no diversion to non-patients.

source.recommendation: CMS 2026: Part B covers influenza, pneumococcal, hepatitis B (risk-based) and COVID-19 vaccines, physician-administered drugs, immunosuppressants after Medicare-covered transplant; Part D covers other ACIP-recommended vaccines (e.g., shingles) with $0 cost-sharing (IRA); 2026 Part D annual out-of-pocket cap $2,100. HRSA 340B: prohibits duplicate discounts and diversion.
